newsitem.title: USA: New ad campaign reaches for newspaper readers.
newsitem.headline: New ad campaign reaches for newspaper readers.

text.p: Television isn't the enemy of newspapers as much as people's fading habit of reading dailies and the declining use of newspapers in classrooms, says a veteran advertising man challenged with trying to reverse newspapers' falling circulation.

These conclusions underlie the new, remedial marketing approach that the Newspaper Publishers Association has launched, according to Jerry & Ketchum, the New York-based advertising agency handed the assignment by the trade group.
"Billings are initially about $5 million but we expect they will go much higher," Jerry Della Femina, majority partner at Jerry & Ketchum, said in an interview.

The campaign recently was launched with ads urging the public to encourage children to read. They will soon be followed by a series of ads with famous people who are faithful readers of newspapers saying how the medium has affected their lives.

"This will be a massive campaign in which the people who run this country will encourage people to read newspapers," Della Femina said. "I expect them to say not only how they respect newspapers but how they like the papers' literacy, how newspapers can help readers become better writers by teaching them grammar, how to construct a sentence and to be aware of what's going on around them."

The task will be a formidable one, judging by the most recent figures released by the Audit Bureau of Circulations. The broad decline in newspaper circulation that started early in the 1990's has continued for most of the country's biggest dailies in the winter months, the ABC reported. Six of the 10 largest newspapers registered declines in the reporting period ended March 31, 1997.
"I don't blame TV," said Della Femina. "It's not the enemy but another way of getting the news which invariably appears first in newspapers."

But he does blame schools for spurning newspapers as a learning medium. "I have an 11-year old daughter who goes to a fancy-shmancy private school in New York," said Della Femina. "I was invited there one day and I asked the teachers why the kids aren't getting newspaper assignments like we used to in my day," he related.
"They hemmed and hawed and said, 'we use the computer instead.' Some said that they didn't read newspapers themselves, so why should they recommend them?"

As part of the new marketing campaign, Della Femina said the publishers' association will advertise on TV as well as in newspapers. "We feel that in newspapers, we are trying to convert the already converted," he said, "but on television we will be talking to many who may have lost the reading habit."

The NPA assignment is "the most exciting I have had in years," said Della Femina, one of the advertising industry's pioneers. I have been a newspaper fan from way back," he added. "I learned how to write by reading columnists like Jimmy Cannon in the New York Post and Jimmy Breslin in several papers," he said.

Della Femina, who has worked in the advertising business for more than three decades, piqued the interest of the NPA when he appeared as a speaker at one of its conventions. "I guess they liked what I told them," he said, "because they came after me with this assignment."
